sentences: Credit utilization is the strongest driver of default risk, accounting for about 27% of the model's importance, and risk generally increases as the share of the credit limit in use rises.
The number of past delinquencies is the second most important driver, with a moderate to strong effect, and default risk jumps once an applicant has at least one delinquency.
The effect of credit utilization grows with the number of past delinquencies, so high utilization is far more damaging for applicants who have had delinquencies.
Income and the length of credit history both have moderate effects, with risk decreasing as income and credit history length rise.
The debt-to-income ratio has a weak to moderate effect, with risk increasing as it rises, and it matters more than the number of dependents.
Recent credit inquiries have at most a weak effect, and age and months at the current address hardly matter.
The data do not settle whether the length of credit history and the number of recent inquiries interact.
Credit utilization does not interact with income in its effect on default risk.
